title: A fair coin from a biased one
objectives: Make a fair bit from a biased coin and find the expected number of flips.

screens.title: A fair coin from a biased one
screens.prose:
Level 5 holds the puzzles interviewers keep asking. Work the same books, easiest first:

- Mosteller, *Fifty Challenging Problems in Probability*: duels and chords
- Zhou, the green book: coins, dice and serial numbers
- Crack, *Heard on the Street*: quick conditioning
- Joshi and co-authors: follow-up questions
- *Probability and Markets*, a free guide from a trading firm

state.caption: One round: two flips of a coin that lands heads with chance $\tfrac23$.

screens.title: Two equal outcomes
screens.prose: A bent coin lands heads with chance $\tfrac23$. You need a fair 50-50 decision. Flip it twice and look at the four outcomes.

state.caption: Each flip: H with $\tfrac23$, T with $\tfrac13$.

screens.question: Tap the two outcomes that have exactly the same chance.

hints.text: HT is $\tfrac23 \times \tfrac13$. Which other path uses the same two numbers?

feedback.correct: HT and TH: each has chance $\tfrac29$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the chance of each path by multiplying.

byKey.repeats: You picked HH and TT. HH has $\tfrac49$ and TT has $\tfrac19$, so they differ.
byKey.h-h: HH has chance $\tfrac49$, more than any other path.
byKey.t-t: TT has chance $\tfrac19$, less than any other path.

explain.text: HT has chance $\tfrac23 \times \tfrac13 = \tfrac29$ and TH has $\tfrac13 \times \tfrac23 = \tfrac29$. The same two factors in a different order give the same product. So call HT heads, call TH tails, and flip again on HH or TT.

screens.title: How many flips?
screens.prose: The pairing you just found is **von Neumann's trick**. Keep HT as heads and TH as tails, and start again on HH or TT. A round keeps a result with chance $\tfrac29 + \tfrac29 = \tfrac49$.

state.caption: Kept: HT and TH. Thrown away: HH and TT.

screens.question: How many flips do you expect to use for one fair decision? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: A round succeeds with chance $\tfrac49$, so the wait is $\tfrac94$ rounds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the expected number of rounds, then double it.

byKey.two: Two flips is one round. Rounds of HH or TT are thrown away, so you need more.
byKey.rounds: That is the number of rounds, $\tfrac94$. Each round costs two flips.
byKey.one-path: You used $\tfrac29$, one kept outcome. A round succeeds on HT or TH, $\tfrac49$.

explain.text: A round of two flips succeeds with chance $\tfrac49$, so we wait $\tfrac94$ rounds on average. That is $2 \times \tfrac94 = \tfrac92 = 4.5$ flips. The thrown-away rounds are the price of fairness.

screens.title: Any bias at all
screens.prose: Drag the point along the curve. It shows the expected flips of the trick for each chance of heads $p$.

derive.caption: At $p$ = {{fixed(p1.x, 2)}}, a round succeeds with chance {{fixed(2 * p1.x * (1 - p1.x), 3)}}: about {{fixed(1 / (p1.x * (1 - p1.x)), 2)}} flips.

screens.question: A coin lands heads with chance 0.6. How many flips does one fair decision take on average? Give four decimal places.

byKey.two: Two flips is one round. Some rounds are thrown away.
byKey.rounds: That is the number of rounds, $\tfrac{1}{0.48}$. Double it for flips.
byKey.fair: That is the fair coin, $\tfrac{1}{0.25}$. Here $pq = 0.24$.

explain.text: HT and TH each have chance $pq = 0.24$, so a round succeeds with 0.48. The trick takes $\tfrac{2}{0.48} = \tfrac{25}{6} \approx 4.1667$ flips. The bit is exactly fair for every $p$ strictly between 0 and 1.

screens.title: The reverse: a die from a coin
screens.prose: Now the coin is fair, and you need a fair choice among six. Three flips give eight equally likely strings. Label six of them 1 to 6, and start again on the other two.

state.caption: Eight strings of three fair flips, each with chance $\tfrac18$.

screens.question: How many flips does one fair choice among six take on average?

hints.text: Each round is three flips. How often does a round succeed?
Six of the eight strings are kept, so a round succeeds with chance $\tfrac68$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the flips per round by the expected rounds.

byKey.three: Three flips is one round. A quarter of rounds land on TTH or TTT and restart.
byKey.rounds: That is the number of rounds, $\tfrac86$. Each round is three flips.
byKey.six: You allowed one flip per face. Three flips already give eight strings.

explain.text: A round of three flips succeeds with chance $\tfrac68 = \tfrac34$, so we expect $\tfrac43$ rounds. That is $3 \times \tfrac43 = 4$ flips. Each face has chance $\tfrac18 \div \tfrac68 = \tfrac16$ once a round succeeds.

screens.title: Two flips cancel the bias?
screens.prose: A candidate answers at once: flip the $\tfrac23$ coin twice. Call HH heads and anything else tails, because two flips average out the bias.
screens.question: How often does this rule say heads?

options.why: You trusted the averaging. Nothing in two flips cancels a bias: HH has chance $p^2$.
That is HH for a fair coin. This coin lands heads with $\tfrac23$.
That is HT, one of the outcomes the pairing trick keeps.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance of HH for this coin.

byKey.b: You trusted the averaging. HH has chance $p^2 = \tfrac49$, so heads is called too rarely.

explain.text: HH has chance $p^2 = \tfrac49$, so the rule calls heads 44% of the time. Only outcomes with equal chances for every $p$ give a fair bit. HT and TH are the pair.

screens.title: The method
screens.prose:
Every round used one fact. Independent flips give $P(HT) = pq = qp = P(TH)$, whatever $p$ is. So keep HT and TH, and flip again on HH or TT. A round of two flips succeeds with chance $2pq$:

$$E[\text{flips}] = \frac{2}{2pq} = \frac{1}{pq}.$$
screens.question: Which coins can the trick turn into a fair bit?

options.why: The bit is exactly fair for any $p$. A strong bias only costs more flips.

options.text: Every coin, a two-headed one too
options.why: With $p = 1$ every round is HH, so no round ever succeeds.

hints.text: A round needs one head and one tail.

feedback.correct: Any coin that can land both ways.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check $p = 1$: what does every round show?

explain.text: The bit is fair for every $p$ strictly between 0 and 1. The edge case is $p = 0$ or $p = 1$: the coin never shows both faces, so the wait $\tfrac{1}{pq}$ is infinite.

screens.title: Why the bit is fair
screens.prose: Put the argument in order, one justified line at a time.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the line that does not belong.

lines.text: Since $pq = qp$, a kept round is heads or tails with chance $\tfrac12$ each.
A round keeps a result with chance $2pq$, so we wait $\tfrac{1}{2pq}$ rounds.
Each round is two flips, so $E[\text{flips}] = \tfrac{1}{pq}$.
The coin is fair on average, so HT and TH balance.
lines.why: The coin is not fair. Independence alone makes the two chances equal.

hints.text: Start from what the flips have in common.
Independence, two products, equality, rounds, flips.

feedback.correct: Independence gives two equal products, then the geometric wait gives the flips.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Begin with independence.

byKey.d1: You used fairness. The coin is biased; independence does the work.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the fairness claim belongs.
byKey.s6: The flip count comes last, after the rounds.

explain.text: Independence makes both kept outcomes a product of $p$ and $q$. Equal products make the bit fair. A geometric wait of $\tfrac{1}{2pq}$ two-flip rounds gives $\tfrac{1}{pq}$ flips.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: Write `von_neumann(flips)` for a string of `'H'` and `'T'`. Read it in pairs: keep `'H'` for HT and `'T'` for TH. Drop HH, TT and any odd last flip. Then write `expected_flips(p)`, returning $\tfrac{1}{pq}$ as a `Fraction`.
screens.question: Write both functions.

widget.how: Check runs 10 hidden tests. Tests 1 to 4 compare the string of bits. Test 5 feeds in 20,000 flips with $p = 0.8$. It needs a share of heads within 0.03 of a half. Test 6 checks about 3,200 bits come out. Tests 7 to 10 need an exact `Fraction`.

hints.text: Step through the string two characters at a time.
`range(0, len(flips) - 1, 2)` gives the start of each full pair.
Keep the first flip of a pair when the two differ. For the wait, `1 / (p * (1 - p))` with `p` a `Fraction`.

feedback.correct: Pairs in, fair bits out, and the exact wait.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the first failing test.

byKey.test-5: The bits are not close to fair. Keep only pairs whose two flips differ.
byKey.test-7: Return a `Fraction`: `1 / (p * (1 - p))` keeps it exact when `p` is one.

explain.text: At $p = 0.8$ a pair is kept with chance $2pq = 0.32$, so 20,000 flips give about 3,200 bits. Each kept bit is heads with chance exactly $\tfrac12$. The wait $\tfrac{1}{pq}$ is $\tfrac92$ at $\tfrac23$ and $\tfrac{25}{6}$ at 0.6.

screens.title: Drill: three more
screens.prose: Drill: about 3 minutes a puzzle, as interviews allow. Keep your own time and say each argument aloud. Give four decimal places.
screens.question: Fill in the three answers.

rows: A coin lands heads with chance 0.9. Expected flips for one fair bit by the trick?
A coin lands heads with chance 0.7. The chance one round of two flips is kept?
A fair coin, and a fair choice among three people. Two flips a round, TT starts again. Expected flips?

hints.text: Each answer uses $2pq$, or the share of strings kept.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c1: Check the first: flips are $\tfrac{1}{pq}$ with $pq = 0.09$.
byKey.r1c1: Check the second: a round is kept on HT or TH, $2pq$.
byKey.r2c1: Check the third: three of four strings are kept, so $\tfrac43$ rounds of two flips.

explain.text: At $p = 0.9$, $\tfrac{1}{0.09} = \tfrac{100}{9} \approx 11.1111$ flips. At 0.7 a round is kept with $2 \times 0.21 = 0.42$. For three people, HH, HT and TH each name one person, so $2 \times \tfrac43 = \tfrac83$ flips.

screens.title: Follow-up: three people
screens.prose: The interviewer extends it: a fair choice among three people, with the 0.6 coin. Flip three times. Keep only HTT, THT and TTH, one person each, and start again otherwise.
screens.question: How many flips does one fair choice take on average? Give four decimal places.

hints.text: Why are the three strings equally likely?
Each has one head and two tails: chance $pq^2 = 0.6 \times 0.16 = 0.096$.
A round succeeds with $3pq^2 = 0.288$, so the flips are $\tfrac{3}{0.288}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the chance a round succeeds, then multiply rounds by three flips.

byKey.one-string: You used one kept string, $pq^2$. A round succeeds on any of the three.
byKey.fair: That is a fair coin, $\tfrac{3}{3/8}$. This coin has $pq^2 = 0.096$.
byKey.two-way: That is the two-way answer. Three people need three equal strings.

explain.text: HTT, THT and TTH each have chance $pq^2$, so they tie for every $p$. A round succeeds with $3pq^2 = 0.288$, giving $\tfrac{3}{0.288} = \tfrac{125}{12} \approx 10.4167$ flips. Fairness costs more than twice the two-way wait.

screens.title: A fair allocation
screens.prose: Two desks must split a scarce bond allocation by a fair toss. The only random source is a counterparty's feed of up-ticks and down-ticks. Ticks are independent, and each is up with chance 0.8.
screens.question: Pairing ticks as in the trick, how many ticks do you expect to read per fair decision?

hints.text: A pair of ticks is kept on up-down or down-up.
A pair is kept with chance $2 \times 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.32$.

byKey.two: Two ticks is one pair. Most pairs are up-up and get thrown away.
byKey.rounds: That is the number of pairs, $\tfrac{1}{0.32}$. Each pair is two ticks.
byKey.fair: That is the wait for a fair source. This feed is biased.

explain.text: A pair is kept with chance 0.32, so 68% of pairs are thrown away. That rejection rate is the price: $\tfrac{1}{0.16} = 6.25$ ticks per decision. The decision is still exactly fair.

ideas: For independent flips, HT and TH both have chance $pq$, so keeping only them gives a fair bit.
A round of two flips succeeds with chance $2pq$, so a fair bit takes $\tfrac{1}{pq}$ flips on average.
Run it in reverse to make any fair choice: keep equally likely strings and start again on the rest.

formula.name: Von Neumann's trick
formula.note: Needs $0 < p < 1$; three equal strings of one head cost $\tfrac{1}{pq^2}$.

summary.trap: Calling HH heads: its chance is $p^2$, not $\tfrac12$. Two flips do not cancel a bias.

quiz.prose: Von Neumann's trick keeps HT as heads and TH as tails.
quiz.question: Why do HT and TH have the same chance?

options.text: The flips are independent, so both chances are $p \times q$
The coin is fair on each flip
options.why: You assumed fairness. The coin is biased, and the trick works anyway.

options.text: Throwing away HH and TT removes the bias
options.why: Throwing outcomes away does not equalise the rest. The two kept outcomes are equal because each is $p \times q$.

options.text: Over many rounds heads and tails even out
options.why: That is the law of averages. Each kept round is fair on its own.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write out the chance of HT and of TH.

explain.text: Independence gives $P(HT) = pq$ and $P(TH) = qp$. These are equal, so the kept bit is fair. Fairness of the coin is never used.

quiz.prose: A coin lands heads every time ($p = 1$). You run the trick.
quiz.question: How many rounds until it gives a bit?

options.text: It never gives one: every round is HH

options.why: Every round shows HH and is thrown away.
That is the fair-coin wait, $\tfrac{1}{2pq}$ at $p = \tfrac12$. Here $pq = 0$, so no round ever succeeds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does every round show?

explain.text: With $p = 1$ every round is HH, so no round succeeds. The formula $\tfrac{1}{pq}$ blows up as $pq$ reaches 0. The trick needs both faces possible.

quiz.prose: A coin lands heads with chance 0.6. You need a fair choice among four people, so you make two fair bits with the trick.
quiz.question: How many flips do you expect to use? Give four decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the flips for one bit, then double it.

byKey.one-bit: That is one bit. Four people need two bits.
byKey.fair: That is a fair coin, $2 \times 4$. Here $pq = 0.24$.

explain.text: One bit costs $\tfrac{1}{0.24} = \tfrac{25}{6}$ flips. Two bits name one of four people, so $\tfrac{25}{3} \approx 8.3333$ flips.
